title: 5. Leading Operational KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk

epigraph.quote: “But definitely, trade receivables in government are not that encouraging.”
epigraph.author: Vijay Gupta, Founder, Chairman and CEO, SoftTech Engineers, Q4 FY2026 earnings call, 2 June 2026

web_blocks.takeaway: Sources: annual reports and decks [15][16][18][19][20][21]; days and unbilled work from my arithmetic on the FY2026 balance sheet [15]. Several KPIs changed definition between reports, which is itself a finding.

web_blocks.html: This dashboard separates the numbers that lead revenue from the numbers that report it. It does not show everything: earlier years of several rows are in older annual reports and decks I did not use, so “not disclosed” here means not in my sources, and the FY2025 revenue figure has three versions (₹96.26 crore in the FY2025 report's narrative [20], ₹95.25 crore consolidated and ₹93.36 crore standalone in its statements [20]). I picked six KPI families because each one answers a question a business like this has to answer: is demand building, is revenue repeating, is cash arriving, is the cost of building product being hidden, is the footprint widening, and is the team productive.

Order book and pipeline. The order book is signed work not yet recognised as revenue; the pipeline is opportunities management says it is bidding for. The book rose from ₹133.6 crore in December 2023 [18] to ₹232.0 crore at March 2026, about 1.7 times FY2026 revenue [15], and ₹302.4 crore at September 2026 [21]. Pipeline went from ₹144.5 crore (India only) to ₹625.6 crore, 4.3 times in under three years. One order carries much of the latest jump: the ₹92.95 crore JNPA port order is 31% of the September book [21]. The book also includes multi-year maintenance and SaaS pieces. The CEO said of a book of “200-odd crores”, about 60% will convert this year and “about 40% recurring” of that [16]. Those splits are management's, not audited.

Recurring revenue. Here the definition problem bites. Pay-per-use and SaaS revenue is the cleanest line: ₹11.75 crore in FY2022 to ₹31.72 crore in FY2026, a 22% five-year growth rate, and up 38.6% in FY2026 on management's base (the audited note's FY2025 figure gives 59%, a difference Chapter 2 explains) [15]. But as a share of sales it only moved from about 20% to about 25%, and in Q2 FY2027 it grew just 11.9% after 55.6% in Q1 (Q1 deck) [21]. Add maintenance contracts and the “recurring” share was 45% in FY2025 and 33% in FY2026; the FY2026 report says plainly “The recurring share therefore fell during the year” and that the move “runs counter” to its 50% objective [15]. The FY2025 report had called the same year's recurring share 24% [20], and the February 2024 deck showed 51% for FY2023 [18]. H1 FY2027 shows 43.5% against 37.5% a year earlier [21]. I would trust the usage-based line and treat the broader share as a moving target.

Collections. The CFO told the June 2026 call that days sales outstanding improved from 372 to 260 [16], and the company's slide shows 462 days in FY2022 (Q4 FY2026 deck) [15]. The data feed's 95 debtor days looks much better, but it counts trade receivables only. The consolidated balance sheet also carries ₹52.8 crore of current contract assets, unbilled work already booked as revenue [15]. Receivables of ₹34.6 crore plus unbilled work come to about 242 days of FY2026 revenue by my arithmetic, close to the company's 260, and about 365 days for FY2025 against its 372. So 60% of the burden is revenue recognised before an invoice is raised. The expected credit loss provision doubled to ₹6.28 crore, 15.4% of gross receivables, from 6.7% (standalone) [15]; management described it as a prudence policy on long-outstanding dues and retention money [16]. Free cash flow after capitalised development was about −₹1.3 crore on the consolidated statements in FY2026, or −₹0.09 crore on the company's own standalone measure [15][27].

Capitalised development. SoftTech writes some of its software engineering cost onto the balance sheet as an asset (an “intangible asset under development”) and expenses it later through amortisation. Additions were ₹15.2 crore in FY2023, ₹32.4 crore in FY2024, ₹32.0 crore in FY2025 and ₹36.5 crore in FY2026, 27% of consolidated revenue [15][20] (FY2024 report for FY2023). FY2026 EBITDA was ₹32.2 crore [16], so had all of that been expensed, EBITDA would have been about −₹4 crore on my arithmetic, though some of the amount may be non-cash. The CEO's defence is that products “generate revenues in subsequent years” and are amortised “within three years or four years” [16]. Amortisation was ₹20.4 crore in FY2026, 15% of revenue [15]. Net intangibles of ₹70.7 crore plus ₹19.6 crore under development equal about 53% of equity [15].

Footprint and runway. The permit footprint went from 340+ live bodies in 2018 [17] to 600+ in 2021 [19] and 1,500+ in 2026 [15], against “substantially more than 4,000” statutory urban local bodies [15]. Cumulative permits went from “1 million+” in 2021 [19] to “more than two million” [15]; at the 2021 deck's “1,000+ permits per day”, five years would add about 1.8 million and the total would be near 2.8 million, so I read the daily figure as a peak, not a run-rate. The company is targeting 300 more government clients [15], but the unserved remainder is the smallest, poorest tier: the annual report itself calls them “the least able to fund discretionary technology” [15]. My arithmetic shows the problem: CivitPERMIT was about half of FY2026 revenue, roughly ₹64 crore, or ₹4.3 lakh per served body per year. Three hundred more clients at that average add about ₹13 crore, against the ₹167 crore gap between FY2026 revenue and the CEO's ₹300 crore target. Client count cannot close that gap alone.

Policy gives a real tailwind to reform-linked spending rather than to software specifically. The Union Cabinet approved a ₹1 lakh crore Urban Challenge Fund in February 2026 with funding tied to reforms including “governance and digital reforms” and a ₹5,000 crore corpus to improve the creditworthiness of 4,223 cities including Tier-II and Tier-III towns (PIB release). The annual report adds Smart Cities, PMAY-Urban 2.0 volumes and India's construction industry growing at about 12% a year [15]. Maharashtra's UDCPR, in force since December 2020, harmonises rules across most of the state (The Hitavada). The company lists BIM-based permits as a growth lever; I did not find a binding national BIM mandate in the sources I read, so I treat BIM as an option, not a tailwind.

Two new revenue streams need a reality check against their own math. CivitTDRx charges 0.5% of each TDR trade on the Mumbai exchange, made mandatory on 10 May 2026; the CEO cited about ₹8,000 crore of TDR trades in the corporation's area in FY2026, and when an analyst computed ₹40 crore a year at that volume, he agreed [16]. Actual H1 FY2027 eTDR revenue was 3.2% of the slide's product total, about ₹2.1 crore, and 5.3% in Q2, about ₹1.8 crore [21]. If all of that were 0.5% fees, Q2 trades would be about ₹366 crore against an implied ₹2,000 crore a quarter. It is early, with a mandate only weeks old and “100-odd registrations” [16], but the ₹40 crore story is unproven. Overseas is a clearer disappointment: outside-India revenue peaked at 4.3% of sales in FY2024 and was ₹2.1 crore, 1.6%, in FY2026 [15][20], and the CEO called Indian products in the US “very, very tough” [16].

Team productivity. Year-end headcount was 582 against 530 a year earlier (+9.8%) while revenue rose 40% [15]. Consolidated revenue per employee therefore rose from ₹18.0 lakh to ₹22.8 lakh, my arithmetic on year-end headcount. The CEO told analysts: “It is not that we will reduce people at this moment, but we can have more growth with the same set of people” [16]. That is a claim to test, since the group's consolidated EBITDA margin was 26.3% in H1 FY2027 against 32.5% standalone, a four-crore EBITDA gap that the company attributes mainly to go-to-market spending in Germany [21].

Before the audit, two corrections to the brief. First, there is no earnings-call history to audit: the 2 June 2026 call was SoftTech's “maiden conference call” [16]. Second, the IPO was not in 2021. The company's prospectus is dated 4 May 2018 for a listing on the NSE EMERGE small-company platform, and it moved to the main boards in 2022 [18]. So the promise record in the table that follows is built from the 2018 deck, the 2021 AGM deck, the February 2024 deck, three annual reports and the June 2026 call. Management turnover matters as well: the CFO who served through FY2025, Kamal Agarwal, resigned on 16 September 2025 and the company secretary on 18 March 2026 [15]. The CFO on the June call, Deepak Bang, was appointed on 17 September 2025 [15], so he is speaking to targets he did not set.

web_blocks.takeaway: Management delivers on one-year growth guidance and on cutting DSO, but long-range targets have been missed or quietly re-dated.

web_blocks.html: Reading the table, a pattern shows. One-year guidance has been credible: FY2026 revenue grew 40% [16], FY2027 guidance of 25-27% is on pace at the standalone level, and DSO fell by 112 days in a year [16]. Multi-year targets are another matter. The $25 million topline appears in the 2021 deck for 2024 with a 25% margin, and in the 2024 deck for 2026 with a 40% margin [19][18]. By June 2026 it had become ₹300 crore in three to four years at 25-30% [16], about $34 million at ₹88/$ (my assumption) and a margin goal reset downward. I would score the CEO as reliable on this year and unreliable on a five-year horizon.

Management's candour on the hard topics deserves credit. The CEO said: “But definitely, trade receivables in government are not that encouraging” [16]. But the same report carries a note, apparently left over from drafting, that its external market-research sources “should be independently verified” before the report is issued [15], and it uses three revenue bases for FY2025. These are small lapses, yet they are exactly the kind of untidiness that deserves a question on the next call.

Walk through one invoice. SoftTech builds a permit system for a state urban department. In the first months it writes code and configures rules for the state's bye-laws; the state has not yet accepted anything, so nothing can be billed. Under the accounting rules the company recognises revenue as work progresses and records the difference as a contract asset, which is simply work done and not yet invoiced. Then come milestones, user acceptance, a payment approval chain, and finally a retention, the 1-2% the CFO described, which the treasury holds back [16]. Each stage is a place where a day becomes a month. That is how a business with ₹133 crore of revenue ends up with ₹88 crore of receivables and unbilled work [15].

If you were sitting across from the CFO, here is what I would ask. How much of the ₹52.8 crore of unbilled work was invoiced in the last six months, and how much has been unbilled for more than a year? What would DSO be if the retention money were excluded? And why did the definition of recurring revenue change between the FY2025 and FY2026 annual reports? Good answers are numbers. Evasive answers are adjectives [15][20].

Munger's line applies: show me the incentive and I will show you the outcome. A company that sets a target for a date three years out, then restates it when the date approaches, is rewarded in every conversation before that date. The practical rule for you is to weight what a management team has delivered over twelve months far more than what it expects to deliver in five years. On that scale SoftTech's FY2026 was a good year: revenue up 40%, DSO down by a third and the order book near ₹230 crore [15][16].

Cash is improving but remains the weak link, because more than half of the receivable burden is unbilled work and the free cash flow is about zero [15]. The cost of building product is large and mostly capitalised, which flatters EBITDA and burdens later profit through amortisation [15]. New streams such as TDR and the port twin are real but small so far [21]. And management's promises are best believed in one-year doses.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Management has shown it can grow fast, trim DSO and sign marquee government contracts. It has not shown that growth turns into free cash, or that five-year targets survive contact with the calendar. Watch three things in the next results: DSO against the 200-day goal, unbilled work, and whether the eTDR line reaches the revenue the CEO described.
